items.body:
## Security fixes

v2.4.0 fixes six vulnerabilities in three servers. Upgrade `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` to 2.3.0,
and `mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-fetch` to 2026.11.11.

| Package | Affected | Fixed in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` | all versions before 2.3.0, and date versions 2025.1.14 through 2026.8.31 | 2.3.0 |
| `mcp-server-git` | through 2026.11.4 | 2026.11.11 |
| `mcp-server-fetch` | through 2026.11.4 | 2026.11.11 |

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` 2.3.0

* **Reads stay with the file that was checked** (Linux and macOS). The read tools and file resources now open a file relative to the directory that was checked, as writes already did, so a directory swapped for a symlink between the access check and the read can no longer return a file from outside the allowed directories. A FIFO, socket or device is refused rather than read. **On Windows this narrows the race without closing it**, as for writes (#5260) ([GHSA-p9cv-8g75-4xcg](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-p9cv-8g75-4xcg))
* **`move_file` moves only the source it checked.** A move within one device first takes the source out of its own checked directory under a fresh name, so a source directory swapped for a symlink can no longer bring an outside file into the allowed directories, where it would become readable ([GHSA-7m4x-rv66-mxhh](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-7m4x-rv66-mxhh))

### `mcp-server-git` 2026.11.11

* **A repository's own Git configuration can no longer make the server run a program.** A read-only call such as `git_status` on an untrusted repository used to run a command named in its `.git/config` (`core.fsmonitor`, `diff.external`, hooks, filter and merge drivers, signing) with the server's privileges. Every Git command now overrides those settings, and a Git older than 2.31, which would ignore the overrides, is refused ([GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2))
* **`--repository` confinement covers alternate object stores, linked worktrees and links in the Git directory.** A repository inside the allowed one could read another repository's objects through `objects/info/alternates`, or pass a linked worktree's Git directory off as the allowed repository's. Both are refused, as is a symlink in a Git directory that leads outside the allowed repository. **On Windows a directory junction is not yet covered** (#5520) ([GHSA-q74p-4wrc-q7w6](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-q74p-4wrc-q7w6))

### `mcp-server-fetch` 2026.11.11

* **IPv6 site-local addresses are private.** The private-address guard read `fec0::/10` as public. It is now refused, and so is any IPv6 address outside global unicast (`2000::/3`) that does not carry an IPv4 address ([GHSA-3rxj-6jhw-qfv7](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-3rxj-6jhw-qfv7))
* **robots.txt is matched against the path the site will resolve**, as well as the path as written, so `//private` or `/x/../private` can no longer get past `Disallow: /private` ([GHSA-f9hh-cmx9-2f23](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-f9hh-cmx9-2f23))

### Upgrading from a date-versioned npm release

The TypeScript servers moved from date versions (2025.x, 2026.x) to semantic versions in 1.0.0. Package managers rank 2.3.0 below every 2025.x and 2026.x version, so they won't offer it as an upgrade. If you are on a date version of `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`, install 2.3.0 explicitly: `npm install @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@2.3.0`.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` | `2.3.0` | npm | **published** |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` | `2.3.0` | npm | **published** |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory` | `2.1.1` | npm | **published** |

| `mcp-server-time` | `2026.11.11` | PyPI | **published** |

items.title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
items.body: In Constitutional AI, a plain-text "constitution" encodes values and gets incorporated into a model via post-training. However, the procedure for creating such a constitution poses significant challenges: who contributes, who decides which norms are included, and to what extent must the process be participatory or democratic? These challenges can be paralyzing. Yet, we argue that taking action is essential: without a deliberate constitution, sovereign models would risk misalignment or default to norms set by frontier model providers. We propose treating the development of a constitution as an evolving, participatory process akin to citizen science, iteratively drafted, tested, and refined. We therefore formulate five desirable principles: iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate. We further argue that such a document must remain responsive not only over time but across the people it governs, and propose that provisions be marked as settled, contested, or underdetermined, so that durable disagreement is recorded in the constitution rather than resolved away. Empirically, we show via agent-based modelling that proposed process for maintaining living constitutions is robust against 50% bad actors among citizens - assuming a share of 75% participants with good intent in the deliberative body. This indicates that the proposed process tolerates a substantial share of adversarial participants.
items.summary: In Constitutional AI, a plain-text "constitution" encodes values and gets incorporated into a model via post-training.

items.title: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules
items.body: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses. Inspired by principle-guided methods such as Constitutional AI, we treat each principle as a voter that compares responses according to that principle, for example, preferring the more helpful or less toxic response. We represent these voters as linear directions in a fixed embedding space, a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. In this linear social choice model, Ge et al. (2024) showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO): From the principles-as-voters lens, this means a response A can be less helpful and more toxic than B, yet still receive a higher reward. We ask whether richer reward models or changes to comparison data can recover PO within loss-based training. We show that PO can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and one-hidden-layer ReLU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) of any fixed width $ d\ge 2 $ with suitable finite parameter bounds. We then recover PO for loss-based training of linear rewards under suitable assumptions in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths. These results motivate dataset design as an approach to recovering PO in constitutional-style alignment while retaining loss-based training.
items.summary: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses.

items.title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
items.body: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Z.AI. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

items.title: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
items.body: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $τ^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.

items.title: HEARSAYBENCH: Can AI Navigate from Abstract Human Rights to Lived Lives?
items.body:
As large language models (LLMs) reach users worldwide, personal counseling has emerged as one of their most consequential applications, sometimes in life-critical situations. Yet broader access does not mean equal support. The text these models learn from disproportionately reflects people with the freedom to act, embedding an implicit assumption that users can leave, report, seek help, or appeal. Existing benchmarks largely inherit this assumption, overlooking users whose agency is constrained by structural conditions such as war, statelessness, and displacement. Meanwhile, models are increasingly shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI, often grounded in ideals like human rights, even as many users live where those rights offer little protection or recourse.
  We introduce HEARSAYBENCH, a human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification grounded in scenarios where structural barriers stand between a person and the exercise of their rights. Built from United Nations and other human rights reports, the scenarios span over 80 regions and cover social, environmental, and personal constraints. Drawing on Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach, HEARSAYBENCH tests whether models can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it. Stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow. Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, yet that knowledge remains hearsay if it cannot translate into advice people can act on. Those people are not alignment's long tail; they are among the users for whom good guidance matters most. HEARSAYBENCH makes this failure measurable, a step toward systems that serve the world as it is rather than as assumed.

## Security: Node.js runtime and CA certificate updates (October 2026)

On October 20, 2026, eMudhra disclosed that the private keys for eight of its intermediate CA certificates could be recovered from the public certificates. On October 21, Node.js shipped [security releases](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases) that update its bundled CA certificates for the compromise and fix several unrelated high-severity runtime CVEs. On October 23, Python's `certifi` 2026.10.23 removed the eMudhra roots `emSign Root CA - C1` and `emSign ECC Root CA - C3`.

**How these servers stand**

- **The TypeScript servers rely on the Node.js runtime for certificate checks.** They ship no CA certificates of their own. Only `server-everything` makes outbound HTTPS requests (`gzip-file-as-resource`), and the Node.js it runs on verifies them. `server-filesystem`, `server-memory` and `server-sequential-thinking` make no network connections.
- **`mcp-server-fetch` verifies HTTPS against the `certifi` bundle**, through `httpx`. Installing from PyPI (`uvx mcp-server-fetch`, `pip install mcp-server-fetch`) resolves the current `certifi`, 2026.10.23 or later. The repository's `fetch` Dockerfile installs from its lockfile, which this release moves to `certifi` 2026.10.23 (#5341).
- **`mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-time` make no network connections.**

**If you run a TypeScript server from npm (`npx` or a global install)**

It runs on your Node.js, which we can't update for you. Please run Node.js **24.22.1 or 26.12.1, or later**, and check with `node --version`. The packages' `engines` field accepts any Node.js 24, so npm won't warn you about an older, unpatched runtime.

**If you run `mcp-server-fetch` from an existing environment**

An environment created before October 23 keeps its older `certifi`. Refresh it with `uvx --refresh mcp-server-fetch`, or `pip install -U certifi`.

items.body:
## Security fixes

v2.1.0 fixes eight vulnerabilities in three servers. Upgrade
`@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` and `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything`
to 2.0.1, and `mcp-server-fetch` to 2026.10.24.

| Package | Affected | Fixed in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` | 1.0.0 through 2.0.0, and date versions through 2026.8.31 | 2.0.1 |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` | 1.0.0 through 2.0.0, and date versions 2025.9.24 through 2026.8.31 | 2.0.1 |
| `mcp-server-fetch` | through 2026.10.19 | 2026.10.24 |

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` 2.0.1

* **Writes stay inside the directory that was checked** (Linux and macOS). A parent directory swapped for a symlink between the access check and the write can no longer redirect `write_file`, `edit_file`, `create_directory` or the `move_file` destination outside the allowed directories. **On Windows this is only partly fixed**; the advisory says what is still exposed and how to configure around it ([GHSA-53mr-w429-c597](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-53mr-w429-c597))
* **Paths are checked exactly as they are used.** The access check no longer strips a trailing quote or whitespace that the file operation keeps, so a sibling directory named after an allowed one with that suffix is no longer reachable ([GHSA-7rgq-gccq-qphx](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-7rgq-gccq-qphx))
* **A symlink spelled in a different letter case no longer passes the symlink check** for a new path on a case-insensitive volume, such as macOS's default. This was a regression in 2026.8.31 ([GHSA-4gxg-m5jx-9j57](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-4gxg-m5jx-9j57))
* **`list_directory_with_sizes` checks each entry before reading its size**, so a symlink inside an allowed directory no longer reveals the size and modification time of a file outside it ([GHSA-hhwq-wxfx-cj7g](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-hhwq-wxfx-cj7g))

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` 2.0.1

* **The HTTP and SSE transports refuse requests from other web origins.** They now check the `Origin` header and no longer send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so a web page the user visits can no longer call the server's tools (such as `get-env`) or read their results ([GHSA-mvf5-2qqv-rg3c](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-mvf5-2qqv-rg3c))

### `mcp-server-fetch` 2026.10.24

* **The address check and the connection use the same host name.** For an internationalized (IDNA) host name, the server used to check one form of the name and connect to another, which could reach an internal address ([GHSA-v38p-wf49-hx2j](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-v38p-wf49-hx2j))
* **NAT64 addresses are judged by the IPv4 address they carry.** An address in `64:ff9b::/96` that wraps a private, loopback or link-local IPv4 address is now refused, as an IPv4-mapped one already was ([GHSA-66qx-2266-pmj6](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-66qx-2266-pmj6))
* **robots.txt is checked again after every redirect**, not only for the URL first requested ([GHSA-3jqg-r5pp-rmp2](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-3jqg-r5pp-rmp2))

### Upgrading from a date-versioned npm release

The TypeScript servers moved from date versions (2025.x, 2026.x) to semantic versions in 1.0.0. Package managers rank 2.0.1 below every 2025.x and 2026.x version, so they won't offer it as an upgrade. If you are on a date version, install 2.0.1 explicitly, for example `npm install @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@2.0.1`.

items.title: Why Does Structured Output Fail? An Empirical Study of Prompt-Enforced Pydantic Schemas Across Nine LLMs
items.body: Pipelines that require structured outputs from hosted language models often specify a Pydantic schema in the prompt, validate the response, and retry when validation fails. Although native structured-output modes provide an alternative, application-side validation remains important for enforcing custom constraints. Yet pipeline reliability is often summarized by a single validity rate, which obscures why outputs fail and which interventions may help. We introduce a fine-grained taxonomy of schema-conformance failures and a deterministic classifier that assigns failure categories from model responses and Pydantic validation errors. We apply this framework to 3,997 generation attempts across nine OpenAI and Anthropic model/API configurations, using questions from HotpotQA and FinanceBench. Our results show that similar validity rates can mask different failure patterns, and that dominant failure categories vary with schema constraints and task. Markdown-fenced JSON is the most common failure: among 681 fenced failures, only 48.0% pass validation after fence removal, while the remainder conceal additional violations, predominantly field-length violations. In an exploratory prompt ablation, variants that suppress fences appear to shift failures toward length violations, but the shift is consistent with exposing violations that were already present, illustrating how aggregate validity rates can obscure changes in failure composition. We derive four engineering practices for validator, schema, retry and evaluation design, three supported by our data and one, on retry feedback, proposed but not tested, and release the classifier, completions, and annotations.

items.title: Invisibilization as a Source of Probability Bias in Language Models
items.body: Language models are aligned to avoid using protected attributes such as race, ethnicity, and gender to inform their responses. Therefore, they increasingly refuse or hedge when such attributes appear in a prompt. However, if a system must decide how much to learn from what people tell it, it is costly to refuse valuable information because of its source. In this article, we measure the cost of declining information in a two-urn game with an exact Bayesian answer. We present leading LLM models from two developers (OpenAI and Anthropic) with a prompt that requires them to decide how far to trust an unverifiable report from a participant whose description we randomize across ten configurations (6,600 sessions). We show that leading models often decline to assess the reporter, treating information as worthless at rates set by the description rather than by the evidence. At its widest, models decline a Black-described reporter 46% of the time and a white-described reporter 9%; yet, when they do assess the information, the Black-described reporter receives slightly more trust. The bias is invisible to audits that compare average trust or look only at assessed cases. It grows with reasoning effort, follows words rather than categories (models invoke race for "Black" but not for its Spanish translation negro, and never for "Indigenous"), and worsens under warning instructions a practitioner would try first. We also present a scoring option that reduces the refusal rate bias. When a model's trust is scored against revealed truth over repeated rounds, it credits identical records equally. In four of five configurations from Anthropic and OpenAI, the racial gap in trust falls below 0.02 by the last rounds.

items.title: From Clinical Judgment to Checkable Rules: Clinician-Led Guardrails for Mental-Health Chatbots
items.body: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in mental-health contexts can be evaluated for safety failures, but the resulting judgments are often difficult to inspect or explain. Common approaches to improving safety rely on prompt engineering, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Constitutional AI. In this work, we describe a clinician-led alternative in which two clinicians define, finalize, and adjudicate the four safety checks of a rule base, which is formally verified for internal consistency and applied as a guardrail over LLM outputs. Here and in the title, clinician-led refers to this rule base, not to the fact extractor or the uncertainty default, which are ours. Every verdict of the resulting verification layer is recomputable from a named rule and sixteen facts. Against an LLM judge matched in model, revision, quantization, rule text, and decoding but without the layer's computed 988/911 fact, the largest disagreement class, the satisfied-rule class, is structured: the Llama-3.3-70B judge, on its primary prompt, demands a crisis resource from 55 of the 65 replies (84.6%) that already contain one, while the same model, asked as a fact extractor, reports a recognized resource present on 54 of the 55. The verification layer never raises that demand, by construction. We report with equal prominence where this judge is stronger: fewer false crisis alarms on the one reference-scored check. We also report the measured cost (a specification revision raised block-class outcomes on held-out boundary prompts of an over-refusal benchmark from 6.0% to 16.0%, chiefly by changing fact extraction), the clinicians' decision to keep our uncertainty default, and the analysis of the result. The contribution is not a safer verdict. It is a guardrail whose disagreements with the judge localize to named rules and facts and whose measured costs trace to named facts and the uncertainty default.

items.title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
items.body: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.

They are on by default and need no setup in the SDK: the spans appear once the application has registered a tracer provider with the OpenTelemetry API, and there are none without one.
